items.prompt: What is the primary cause of an earthquake?

options.label: Sudden slip along a fault in the Earth's crust
options.feedback: Correct. An earthquake happens when rocks on either side of a fault suddenly slip past each other, releasing built-up stress as seismic waves.

options.label: Volcanic eruption pushing magma upward
options.feedback: Volcanic eruptions can trigger small quakes, but the main cause of earthquakes is fault slip, not the movement of magma itself.

options.label: Movement of the Earth's magnetic field
options.feedback: The magnetic field is generated in the outer core and has nothing to do with the shaking of the ground; earthquakes are from rock movement.

options.label: The Moon's gravitational pull on the crust
options.feedback: The Moon's gravity causes tides, not earthquakes. Earthquakes come from stress released along faults.

items.ko_line: Fault slip, not magma or tides.
items.exp_text: Earthquakes occur when rocks along a fault suddenly slip, releasing stored elastic energy as seismic waves that shake the ground.

items.prompt: What is a fault in geological terms?

options.label: A crack in the crust with no movement
options.feedback: A crack without movement is called a joint, not a fault. Faults involve displacement of rock on either side.

options.label: A large underground cavern filled with water
options.feedback: A water-filled cavern is a cave, not a fault. Faults are fractures where rocks have moved.

options.label: A fracture in the Earth's crust where rocks have moved past each other
options.feedback: Correct. A fault is a fracture along which there has been relative movement of the rock blocks, often leading to earthquakes.

options.label: A boundary between two separate tectonic plates
options.feedback: Plate boundaries may contain faults, but a fault is specifically a fracture with movement, not the boundary itself.

items.exp_text: A fault is a fracture in rock where the two sides have been displaced relative to each other, often causing earthquakes when slip occurs.

options.label: In the middle of continental interiors
options.feedback: Most quakes are not in continental interiors; they are rare there because these areas are far from plate boundaries.

options.label: Along plate boundaries and fault lines
options.feedback: Correct. Most earthquakes happen at or near plate boundaries where plates interact, and along associated fault lines.

options.label: Under the ocean floor, far from any boundary
options.feedback: The ocean floor far from boundaries is usually quiet; earthquakes concentrate at boundaries, not in quiet interiors.

options.label: In the Earth's core, deep below the crust
options.feedback: Earthquakes originate in the crust and upper mantle, not in the core, which is too deep and fluid.

items.exp_text: Earthquakes predominantly occur along plate boundaries and fault zones where tectonic plates interact, building and releasing stress.

items.prompt: What is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's origin called?

options.label: Epicenter
options.feedback: Correct. The epicenter is the surface point directly above the focus (hypocenter), where the quake's shaking is typically strongest.

options.label: Focus
options.feedback: The focus (hypocenter) is the point below the surface where the rock slips, not the surface point above it.

options.label: Fault plane
options.feedback: The fault plane is the fracture surface itself, not a surface point. The epicenter is a specific location on the ground.

options.label: Seismic wave source
options.feedback: Seismic waves originate at the focus, but the surface point above is specifically the epicenter, not a general source.

items.exp_text: The epicenter is the location on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's focus, where damage is often greatest.

items.prompt: What type of seismic wave arrives first at a seismograph after an earthquake?

options.label: Surface wave
options.feedback: Surface waves travel along the ground and arrive last, after body waves; they are slowest but often most damaging.

options.label: S-wave
options.feedback: S-waves (secondary waves) arrive after P-waves because they travel slower; they cannot pass through liquids.

options.label: P-wave
options.feedback: Correct. P-waves (primary waves) are the fastest seismic waves, so they reach seismographs first, before S-waves and surface waves.

options.label: Love wave
options.feedback: Love waves are a type of surface wave, arriving later; they are not the first to be recorded.

items.exp_text: P-waves are compressional waves that travel fastest through rock, so they are the first to be detected after an earthquake.

items.prompt: What is the shaking of the ground during an earthquake actually caused by?

options.label: The ground moving up and down like an ocean wave
options.feedback: Seismic waves can have up-and-down motion, but they are energy traveling through rock, not actual water waves.

options.label: Magma flowing below the crust
options.feedback: Magma movement may cause volcanic tremors, but the shaking of a typical earthquake is from seismic waves, not magma.

options.label: The whole planet tilting slightly
options.feedback: Earthquakes do not tilt the whole planet; the shaking comes from localized wave motion along the fault.

options.label: Seismic waves traveling through the ground
options.feedback: Correct. The shaking is the passage of seismic waves, which are energy released from the fault slip, moving through the Earth.

items.exp_text: Earthquake shaking is the direct result of seismic waves, which spread outward from the focus, causing the ground to vibrate.

items.prompt: Why do aftershocks happen after a large earthquake?

options.label: They are caused by aftershocks of the aftershocks
options.feedback: That's just recursive; aftershocks happen because the main quake changes stress on nearby faults, not because of a chain of aftershocks.

options.label: The main quake redistributes stress on nearby faults
options.feedback: Correct. The main earthquake changes the stress in the surrounding rock, causing other faults to slip in smaller earthquakes as they adjust.

options.label: The Earth's crust continues to move because of the magnetic field
options.feedback: Magnetic field changes do not cause earthquakes; aftershocks are due to stress adjustments, not magnetism.

options.label: Magma continues to rise after the quake
options.feedback: Aftershocks are not related to magma; they occur on faults near the original rupture from stress changes.

items.exp_text: Aftershocks occur because the main quake alters stress on nearby faults, making them slip again in smaller events as the crust adjusts.

items.prompt: What is the point inside the Earth where an earthquake starts called?

options.label: Epicenter
options.feedback: The epicenter is on the surface, not inside. The start point underground is a different term.

options.label: Seismograph location
options.feedback: A seismograph is a surface instrument that records waves, not where the quake begins.

options.label: Fault line
options.feedback: A fault line is the surface trace of a fault, not the point of origin underground.

options.label: Focus (hypocenter)
options.feedback: Correct. The focus, also called the hypocenter, is the underground point where the rock first slips and energy is released.

items.exp_text: The focus (hypocenter) is the exact location below ground where an earthquake rupture begins, from which seismic waves radiate.

options.label: A series of large ocean waves caused by sudden displacement of water
options.feedback: Correct. Tsunamis are giant waves generated by abrupt water displacement, often from underwater earthquakes, landslides, or volcanic eruptions.

options.label: A giant wall of water caused by the Moon's gravity
options.feedback: Tides are from the Moon's gravity, but tsunamis are from sudden displacement, not tidal forces.

options.label: A single enormous wave that travels across the ocean surface
options.feedback: Tsunamis are a series of waves, not just one, and they travel through the whole water column, not just on the surface.

options.label: A wave that only happens during high tide
options.feedback: Tsunamis are unrelated to tides; they occur from any sudden water displacement, regardless of tidal stage.

items.exp_text: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves with very long wavelengths, caused by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water.

items.prompt: What instrument is used to detect and record seismic waves?

options.label: Barometer
options.feedback: A barometer measures air pressure, not ground motion. Seismic waves need a seismograph.

options.label: Seismograph
options.feedback: Correct. A seismograph detects and records the vibrations of the ground caused by seismic waves during an earthquake.

options.label: Thermometer
options.feedback: A thermometer measures temperature, which is unrelated to detecting seismic waves.

options.label: Compass
options.feedback: A compass detects magnetic fields and gives direction, not seismic waves.

items.exp_text: A seismograph is a sensitive instrument that detects ground motion from seismic waves, producing a seismogram record.
